newsitem.title: FRANCE: French parliament faces stormy immigration debate.
newsitem.headline: French parliament faces stormy immigration debate.

text.p: The French parliament debates a hotly-disputed immigration bill from Tuesday as thousands of intellectuals and artists protest in a struggle fought in the shadow of the far-right National Front.
Campaigners who marched through Paris on Saturday have called a new demonstration close to the National Assembly (lower house) to put pressure on deputies as they launch their three-day debate.
In Lyons, Grenoble and Aix-en-Provence, left-wing groups staged new rallies on Monday against the proposed new bill.

After a flurry of petitions led by film makers, artists, writers and academics, the government withdrew the bill's most controversial clause. The opposition Socialists pledged to use all possible procedural tricks to defeat the bill.

The clause, intended to prevent people from developing countries from overstaying short-term visas and turning into illegal immigrants, ordered their French hosts to notify police of their departure. The government has now agreed to make the foreigners responsible for reporting their own departure.
Immigration is turning into the hottest issue just over a year ahead of general elections as the government and protesters accuse each other of pandering to the anti-immigrant Front.

Organisers of Tuesday's protest said it would mark a step in a nationwide campaign against hardline immigration laws. "There is no question of abandoning this citizens' struggle, whether the law goes through or not," said writer Dan Franck.

Tens of thousands of intellectuals, artists, left-wing politicians and ordinary citizens took part in the Paris march, but the ruling RPR Gaullist party described the demonstration and small protests in other cities as "a stinging failure".

RPR secretary-general Jean-Francois Mancel, referring to opinion polls showing a majority of the public backed the bill, said: "The French people have shown common sense with a wide majority backing the government's position of fighting against illegal immigration while scrupulously respecting human rights."

According to a survey published by the newspaper Le Monde, 80 percent of the Paris demonstrators were not members of political parties or trade unions. But 84 percent said they felt closest to the Left or to environmentalists.

The IFOP poll, based on questioning of 3,322 marchers, showed that the victory of the far-right and anti-immigration National Front in the depressed southern town of Vitrolles this month had been the catalyst for 59 percent of them.
Catherine Megret, the new Vitrolles mayor, said in an interview with a German newspaper that France was in a state of emergency and the Front wanted to instil fear in immigrants.

A political newcomer who ran in place of her husband, Front number two Bruno Megret, the new mayor told the Berliner Zeitung she would cut almost all social payments to immigrants and fire social workers to hire more police for a crime crackdown.
Pro-immigrant groups would lose their subsidies and most left-wing books would be removed from municipal libraries, she said. Rap and black musicians would also be unwelcome.
The Socialist party denounced Megret's interview as representing "a policy of racist inspiration".

"When you put together the references to differences between races, the discriminatory policy on welfare payments and the policy aimed at subsidising only French or rightist groups, then you can see it all adds up to representing the very principles of racism and of segregation," Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande told reporters.
Socialist leader Lionel Jospin on Sunday hailed the dropping of the controversial immigration clause but did not say whether he was still pressing for the complete withdrawal of the bill.

According to another poll published by the newspaper Le Figaro, a 59 to 34 percent majority of French people want the government to maintain the bill. But they were divided evenly on the protesters' call for civil disobedience if it became law, the IPSOS survey said.
